sources_considered.why: Original probability-based polling, fielded in May 2026 and published before the evaluation date, includes comparable prior-year measures.
Original research summary reports growth in organized opposition during January–March 2026.
Dated June 13 coverage establishes that the Q1 findings were public before the post and identifies multiple concerns.
Original international survey report supplies material geographic qualifications. Unclear fieldwork dates prevent using it as decisive target-period evidence.
Readable examples were considered, but systematic polling and opposition records provide stronger evidence.

evidence_items.locator: Opening summary; sections on harm, trust and jobs; Survey Methods
evidence_items.explanation: The May 4–11 survey found that Americans saying AI does more harm than good rose from 31% to 39% year over year; expected job losses also increased and trust declined. These changes support growing negative sentiment, though Gallup describes some shifts as modest.

The Q1 summary documents a substantial increase in organized opposition, alongside blocked or delayed projects. June 13 is the verified public-availability bound supplied by e3; the original summary page does not state its publication day.

evidence_items.locator: Second article paragraph; publication date above article
evidence_items.explanation: This contemporaneous article reports the Q1 disruption findings and identifies electricity costs, water use and noise among residents' concerns. It corroborates the timing and multiple-concern aspect, but is not independent of Data Center Watch's project counts.

The report describes worsening US and UK sentiment while finding substantially more positive attitudes in emerging economies and Asian countries. This limits any worldwide reading; its October 8 update and unspecified fieldwork dates prevent treating it as decisive evidence for the first-half window.

unresolved_gaps: No single measure defines really intense.
The evidence is strongest for the United States and does not establish uniform worldwide intensification.
Data-center opposition can concern local infrastructure impacts without implying rejection of AI generally.
